title: High-Content Drug Screening Using Tumor Organoids on a 384-Pillar Plate Platform
author: Choi, Lee, et al.
materials: Matrigel is a thermosensitive ECM hydrogel that rapidly polymerizes above 10°C. Proper handling is critical for consistent organoid morphology and imaging quality.7.Thaw Matrigel slowly at 4°C overnight.a.Do not thaw at room temperature (20°C–25°C), as this leads to premature gelation.8.On the day of use, maintain all Matrigel and related materials on ice, including pipettes, pipette tips, tubes, and plates.9.Pre-cool all consumables and equipment (pipette tips, 384-pillar plates, microcentrifuge tubes) to 4°C before use.10.Handle Matrigel slowly and gently using wide-bore or cut tips to avoid introducing air bubbles.Note: Matrigel rapidly solidifies at >10°C. Strict temperature control is essential for consistency and reproducibility.CRITICAL: Avoid bubble formation when pipetting Matrigel. steps.title: Thaw and expand SKOV-3 cells
steps.instruction: Thaw frozen SKOV-3 cells in a 37 °C water bath for 1–2 min until a small ice crystal remains, then transfer 5.0 × 10⁵ cells per flask to 9 mL pre‑warmed complete McCoy’s 5A medium (445 mL base medium + 50 mL FBS + 5 mL penicillin‑streptomycin). Wash once to remove DMSO, plate in T25 or T75 flasks, and incubate at 37 °C, 5 % CO₂, changing medium every 2–3 days.

steps.title: Subculture SKOV-3 to required density
steps.instruction: When cultures reach ~80–90 % confluency, aspirate medium, rinse once with sterile PBS, add 1 mL 0.25 % Trypsin‑EDTA, incubate 37 °C 3–5 min until cells round, neutralize with 9 mL complete medium, collect suspension, centrifuge ~300 × g 5 min, aspirate supernatant, resuspend pellet in fresh medium, and seed new T75 flasks at the desired density; keep cells below passage 30 and test for mycoplasma.

steps.title: Prepare Matrigel on ice
steps.instruction: Thaw growth‑factor‑reduced Matrigel (Corning #354230) slowly at 4 °C overnight; keep all Matrigel, pipette tips, tubes, and plates on ice (or at 4 °C) during handling, use wide‑bore or cut tips, and avoid bubbles.

steps.title: Design 384‑well plate layout
steps.instruction: Create a 384‑well layout excluding outer rows (A, P) and columns (1, 24); test each compound at seven concentrations in triplicate; assign positive‑control wells (e.g., Staurosporine or Cisplatin) and negative‑control wells (untreated cells) in the central region; use the same layout for all replicates.

steps.title: Aliquot and store compound library
steps.instruction: Obtain compounds as 10 mM DMSO stocks, aliquot into low‑binding polypropylene 96‑ or 384‑well plates, seal and store at –20 °C (up to 6–12 months) or 4 °C (up to 1–2 weeks), minimize freeze‑thaw cycles, thaw at room temperature (20–25 °C) before use, and mix gently.

steps.title: Set up equipment and pre‑cool plates
steps.instruction: Set laboratory temperature to 22–25 °C, pre‑warm CO₂ incubators to 37 °C, pre‑cool empty 384‑well plates at 4 °C, and pre‑warm a 384‑well plate filled with medium in the incubator.

steps.title: Harvest and count SKOV-3 cells
steps.instruction: Grow SKOV‑3 cells in a T‑75 flask to ~80–90 % confluency, aspirate medium, rinse with 5 mL pre‑warmed PBS (no Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺), add 1 mL 0.25 % Trypsin‑EDTA, incubate 37 °C 2–3 min, tap flask if needed, neutralize with 9 mL complete medium, transfer to a 15 mL tube, centrifuge 300 × g 3 min at 20–25 °C, aspirate supernatant, resuspend pellet in 10 mL medium, count cells with trypan blue, ensure viability > 90 %, and dilute to 1.0 × 10³ cells per 1.5 µL (6.67 × 10⁵ cells mL⁻¹). Keep suspension on ice or at 20–25 °C and use within 30 min.

steps.title: Mix cells with Matrigel (3:7 v/v)
steps.instruction: In a pre‑chilled 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube, combine 30 µL cell suspension (6.67 × 10⁵ cells mL⁻¹) with 70 µL cold Matrigel, mix gently 5–6 times with wide‑bore tips, preparing ~10 % excess to account for dead volume; avoid bubbles.

steps.title: Dispense mixture onto each pillar
steps.instruction: Pre‑cool the 384‑pillar plate on ice or a 4 °C block for ≥10 min; using a pre‑chilled low‑volume dispenser (e.g., ASFA® SPOTTER), dispense 1.5 µL of the cell‑Matrigel mixture onto the center of each pillar; keep the plate at 4 °C for 10 min to let cells settle by gravity without disturbance.

steps.title: Polymerize Matrigel and mount pillar plate
steps.instruction: Equilibrate the pillar plate at room temperature (20–25 °C) for 10–15 min, then transfer to a 37 °C incubator for 40 min for complete polymerization; pre‑warm 60 µL complete McCoy’s 5A medium in each well of a matching 384‑well receiver plate (deep‑well U‑bottom preferred), align and gently press the polymerized pillar plate onto the receiver plate to ensure uniform contact.

steps.title: Incubate organoids for 24 h
steps.instruction: Place the assembled pillar‑receiver plate in a 37 °C, 5 % CO₂ incubator for 24 h without shaking or moving to allow spheroid formation and baseline maturation.

steps.title: Assess organoid uniformity (optional)
steps.instruction: After 24 h, acquire bright‑field or fluorescence images, discard wells with edge effects, absent organoids, or imaging artifacts, calculate coefficient of variation (CV %) across replicates, and exclude plates with CV > 10 % from further analysis.

steps.title: Prepare 4 µM Calcein‑AM staining solution
steps.instruction: Make a 1 mM Calcein‑AM stock in DMSO, store at –20 °C protected from light; immediately before use, dilute the stock in pre‑warmed PBS (37 °C) to 4 µM, mix gently without vortexing, and keep under low light, using within 30 min.

steps.title: Stain organoids with Calcein‑AM
steps.instruction: After the 72 h drug incubation (assumed completed), detach the organoid‑loaded pillar plate from the drug plate, place it onto a fresh 384‑well plate containing 40 µL per well of 4 µM Calcein‑AM, and incubate 1 h at 37 °C, 5 % CO₂ without shaking.

steps.title: Wash organoids three times with PBS
steps.instruction: Transfer the pillar plate sequentially to three fresh 384‑well plates, each filled with 60 µL PBS per well; let passive diffusion occur for 15 min per wash at 20–25 °C, avoiding pipetting or agitation to preserve Matrigel structure.

steps.title: Acquire fluorescence images
steps.instruction: Mount the stained pillar plate on an imaging‑compatible 384‑well receiver plate containing 60 µL PBS per well; image with an automated fluorescence microscope (e.g., ASFA SCANNER) using a FITC/GFP filter (Ex ≈ 488 nm, Em ≈ 520 nm) and the following settings: shutter speed 15 ms, gain 2, objective 4× or 10×; acquire images suitable for organoid depth (Z‑stack if available).

steps.title: Process images and quantify intensity
steps.instruction: Import images into analysis software (e.g., ASFA SCANNER, ImageJ), exclude wells with edge effects or artifacts, apply automated segmentation to identify each organoid, measure total or average Calcein‑AM fluorescence intensity per organoid, and export raw intensity data for all wells.

steps.title: Normalize viability data using controls
steps.instruction: Set the average intensity of negative‑control wells (media only, no cells) as 0 % viability and the average intensity of positive‑control wells (untreated cells) as 100 % viability; calculate relative viability for each drug‑treated well as % = (F_sample – F_NEG) / (F_POS – F_NEG) × 100.

steps.title: Generate dose‑response curves and IC50
steps.instruction: Import normalized viability data into GraphPad Prism (or equivalent), plot % viability versus compound concentration, fit a variable‑slope sigmoidal dose‑response model, and extract IC₅₀ values with confidence intervals for each compound.

description: Tumors are composed of spatially complex and heterogeneously organized cellular populations, creating a microenvironment that significantly influences cell behavior, drug response, and therapeutic efficacy.1,2,3 Traditional two-dimensional (2D) cell culture models, while simple and reproducible, have inherent limitations in recapitulating the structural organization and microenvironmental interactions observed in tumors.4,5 These limitations ultimately weaken the predictive value of drug screening and therapeutic evaluations.6,7 To overcome these limitations, three-dimensional (3D) culture systems, such as spheroids and organoids, have emerged as more physiologically relevant in vitro models.8,9,10 These systems better mimic the tumor microenvironment, enabling more accurate prediction of in vivo drug behavior and supporting translational cancer research.11,12,13 Consequently, in response to this development, there is an increasing need to develop 3D organoid-based high-throughput screening (HTS) platforms, which can facilitate large-scale and more accurate drug screening, offering greater potential for precision medicine and drug discovery in cancer research.14,15,16,17 However, conventional dome-based 3D cultures remain constrained by technical challenges that limit their scalability and automation compatibility, including variability in dome size, high reagent consumption, and difficulty in handling viscous matrices. To address these limitations, we developed a miniaturized 3D organoid culture platform compatible with automated liquid handling and high-content imaging systems for scalable drug screening. The following protocol outlines this approach using a vertical 384-pillar plate format.
